items.title: DAISY
items.text:
Safe use of AI in companies

Data Protection and Employee Interests in AI-as-a-Service Systems

AI has become an important tool in many companies. DAISY aims to research service solutions that are practical while minimizing privacy risks: technically, psychologically and organizationally, tested in everyday business operations.

items.title: Project summary
items.text:
Many companies use artificial intelligence as a service: employees query an internally configured chatbot whose language model is operated in the cloud by a third-party provider. This is cheap, fast, and requires hardly any in-house AI expertise. In other enterprises, an AI strategy might not even have been laid out yet and employees are using various unpoliced personal tools.

What remains open is what happens to employees' data, who bears responsibility and where the limits of the system lie - especially when automating workflows with agentic tools. These risks are rarely intuitive for users and decision-makers, as they differ significantly from the commercial chatbots people know from their private lives.

DAISY starts exactly there. As a consortium of computer science, psychology and practice, we develop IT security solutions, strengthen the competence of decision-makers and employees, and shape the introduction of AI services in Ruhr area companies together in a participatory and transparent way. The legal framework is taken into account from the very beginning.

items.title: Latest news
items.text:
All news

  • Secure technology

    We build on open-source tools and test configurations that address typical privacy risks of AIaaS. Interactive demonstrators make them tangible.

  • Sound insights

    We investigate how employees and decision-makers understand AIaaS, and compare these mental models with the actual properties of the systems.

  • Practical processes

    We develop evidence-based process models for a calibrated, employee-centered introduction of AI services, tailored to the organizational culture.

  • Free use

    We make all results available under an open license and free of charge. No separate patent or property right applications are planned.

items.text:
Courtesy translation

This is a courtesy translation. The German version of this page is legally binding.

items.title: We do not collect any personal data ourselves
items.text:
DAISY is a static website. It is built from Markdown sources and delivered as plain HTML, CSS and image files. There is:

  • no tracking – no analytics, no cookies, no measurement of usage behavior,
  • no external resources – no web fonts, no scripts and no stylesheets from third parties; all files come from our own domain,
  • no server log analysis for analytics or advertising purposes,
  • no forms collecting personal data – contact is made via an e-mail address that you use yourself in your mail program.

You can verify this yourself: when loading this page, only files from its own domain daisy.ruhr are loaded.

items.title: Hosting
items.text:
The website is hosted by statichost.eu (Variable Object Assignment, c/o Knackeriet, Sankt Paulsgatan 25, 118 48 Stockholm, Sweden). For delivery, statichost.eu uses servers of Hetzner Online GmbH (Germany) and the content delivery network of BunnyWay d.o.o. (Slovenia).

When you visit the website, your IP address is processed for technical reasons in order to deliver the requested files to your device. According to the host, no personal data is stored in log files; only technical details such as time, requested address and data volume are logged and kept for at most 7 days. The legal basis is Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR – legitimate interest in providing the website securely and reliably. The host processes this data on our behalf (Art. 28 GDPR); no transfer to countries outside the EU/EEA takes place. Details are governed by the statichost.eu privacy policy.

The source code of the website is stored on GitHub (GitHub Inc., USA). Visiting the website does not transfer any data to GitHub; GitHub's privacy policy only applies if you follow the link to the source code.

items.title: Project team
items.text:
DAISY connects computer science, psychology and practice. The consortium comprises three scientific partners and one practice partner; four associated partners contribute as multipliers and dialogue partners without funding of their own.

Photo left to right: Dr. Steffen Becker (RUB), Gregor Mähler (WirtschaftsEntwicklungsGesellschaft Bochum mbH), Dr. Greta Ontrup (UDE), Dr. Alina Tausch (Uni Witten-Herdecke), Dr. Magdalena Wischnewski (UDE).

items.title: RUB – Ruhr University Bochum
items.text: Focus on the technical subsystem: security and data protection architectures of AIaaS systems, empirical system analysis, demonstrators.

items.title: Dr.-Ing. Steffen Becker
items.text:
Technology

I lead DAISY’s technical subproject at Ruhr University Bochum. My research combines IT security and human-computer interaction. In DAISY, we examine the actual privacy risks of AI-as-a-Service systems and develop safeguards that are technically robust and practical in everyday work.

items.title: UW/H – Witten/Herdecke University
items.text: Organizational link between the social and the technical subsystem: decision-making and negotiation processes, process models for calibrated AIaaS introductions.

items.title: Dr. Alina Tausch
items.text:
Organizational psychology

I am leading the organizational psychology component of the project, currently from the University of Witten/Herdecke. Drawing on my research at the intersection of work design and organizational psychology, I examine - as a business psychologist - how decision-makers in organizations decide about AI and what role organizational factors, such as organizational culture, play.

items.title: Lukas Bring
items.text:
PhD - Organizational psychology

As a psychologist and research associate at Witten/Herdecke University within the DAISY project, I focus on the organizational psychology of decision-making when companies adopt AI-as-a-Service systems. I investigate the criteria decision-makers use when they select and introduce these systems, how they weigh opportunities against risks, and what role data protection and employees’ interests play in those decisions. The goal is to better understand how organizations can introduce AI systems responsibly, with care for data privacy and for the people who work with them.

items.title: UDE – University of Duisburg-Essen
items.text: Social subsystem and individual level: mental models of AIaaS users, intervention formats for competence development.

items.title: Dr. Greta Ontrup
items.text:
Psychology

Together with Dr. Magdalena Wischnewski, I lead the project’s work and organizational psychology part. I bring expertise in human-AI teaming and in how data-driven business processes affect employees. In DAISY, I study how employees perceive systems delivered as a service. I focus especially on the risks that come from employees’ own beliefs and interpretations about data protection and privacy.

items.title: Dr. Magdalena Wischnewski
items.text:
Psychology

I lead the junior research group on human factors in AI systems. In my research, I examine what it means to "trust AI". In the DAISY project, I contribute to the individual psychology perspective by investigating how employees make sense of intelligent systems and how this is reflected in their interaction with them.

items.title: Muazzez Deniz Barut
items.text:
PhD - Psychology

I am a PhD researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen, focusing on the psychological aspects of human-AI interaction. In DAISY, I investigate how employees understand AI-as-a-Service systems and the mental models they develop about how these systems work, as well as the associated privacy and security risks. The goal is to identify potential misconceptions and promote informed and privacy-conscious AI use in the workplace.

items.title: BoWE – WirtschaftsEntwicklungsGesellschaft Bochum mbH
items.text: Practice partner in a dual role: implements solutions operationally as pilot user and acts as a regional multiplier in Bochum's business community and city administration.

items.title: Gregor Mähler
items.text:
Practice

I lead the DAISY project at Bochum Economic Development, focusing on secure, privacy-compliant AI-as-a-Service and its practical applications. Together with our university partners, I assess technical and organisational requirements and share the findings with other businesses.

items.title: Using AI safely in companies
items.text:
DAISY explores how companies can use cloud-based AI services while protecting sensitive data and taking employees' interests into account.

From left: Dr. Steffen Becker, Gregor Mähler, Dr. Greta Ontrup, Dr. Alina Tausch and Dr. Magdalena Wischnewski.

Hardly any company can afford to ignore artificial intelligence anymore. Those without an in-house solution often turn to commercial AI services. Yet it is often unclear what happens to the data processed by these providers. The DAISY collaborative project helps companies use AI responsibly. Researchers from the universities of Bochum, Duisburg-Essen, and Witten/Herdecke will examine use cases, develop technical solutions for the secure use of AI, and take organizational and individual psychological aspects into account. All results will be made publicly available. Starting in September 2026, the consortium will receive €1.29 million in funding over three years from the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space as part of the “Privacy Platform” funding initiative.

items.title: Cooperation partners
items.text: In addition to Ruhr University Bochum, which coordinates the consortium, the project partners are the University of Duisburg-Essen, Witten/Herdecke University, and WirtschaftsEntwicklungsGesellschaft Bochum.

items.title: Balancing efficiency and data protection
items.text: “Many companies have valuable data that, until now, hardly anyone has been able to use systematically. Artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing that,” says project coordinator Dr. Steffen Becker from the Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security at Ruhr University Bochum. Whether it is answering customer inquiries, summarizing contracts, or taking meeting minutes, AI applications can make many everyday tasks easier and faster – and in doing so, they almost always access internal documents as well as customer or employee data. “We are therefore always balancing the efficiency gains offered by AI against the need to protect sensitive data,” says Steffen Becker.

items.title: Technical solutions
items.text: The research team will first take a close look at how AI is actually being used in companies before developing solutions for its secure deployment. “Once data has been transferred to an AI service, it is almost impossible to fully understand from the outside what happens to it. We therefore want to systematically examine the actual data protection risks associated with commonly used services – and provide companies with tools that prevent sensitive data from being transferred without proper checks in the first place,” Steffen Becker explains. The researchers are considering, for example, filtering solutions that identify confidential information before it leaves the company and either warn users or block its transmission.

items.title: The right balance of trust and skepticism
items.text:
Researchers at Witten/Herdecke University are examining AI-related processes within companies from an organizational psychology perspective. How, for example, do company management teams make decisions? What attitudes do works councils have toward AI? Researchers at the University of Duisburg-Essen are focusing on employees and contribute the individual psychology perspective. “What matters is that people neither trust AI blindly nor underestimate what it can do,” says Dr. Magdalena Wischnewski. “We are therefore investigating what ideas employees have about how AI works, where misconceptions arise, and how an appropriate level of trust can be fostered,” adds Dr. Greta Ontrup. Both researchers lead Young Investigator Groups at the Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security (RC Trust) at the University of Duisburg-Essen. Among other things, the researchers will develop training formats based on these findings. “We are also addressing the legal aspects through a legal opinion, particularly the interplay between data protection, the AI Act, and labor law,” says Steffen Becker.

Editorial note: This article was originally published by Ruhr University Bochum. This English version has been supplemented with quotes from RC Trust researchers Dr. Magdalena Wischnewski and Dr. Greta Ontrup at the University of Duisburg-Essen and was originally published on the RC Trust page and authored by Meike Drießen: Using AI safely in companies, published on 29 September 2026.
